sources.fullCitation: Deutsche Nationalbibliothek. “Mann, Paul.” Gemeinsame Normdatei, GND 133442284.
sources.researchNote: The GND records the composer as born in Vienna in 1910 and deceased in New York on 27 May 1983. It gives the variants Wechselmann, Paul; Mawersky, Paul Stephan; Bachinger, Alois; Marois, Jean; and Walden, Peter, and links BnF ark:/12148/cb14768347k, LCNAF nb2003055670, VIAF 3662538 and Wikidata Q31202678. The Library of Congress heading reads “Mann, Paul, 1910–1983” and cites the 1944 sheet “Tell me I’m the only one you care for”. The day and month of birth are contested: German Wikipedia gives 3 September 1910 while the GND gives 3 October 1910; both agree on the year and on the death date.
sources.title: GND 133442284 — Mann, Paul
sources.creator: Deutsche Nationalbibliothek

sources.shortCitation: GND and LCNAF authority records for Robert Péguy
sources.fullCitation: Deutsche Nationalbibliothek. “Péguy, Robert.” Gemeinsame Normdatei, GND 1061685829. Library of Congress. “Péguy, Robert, 1883–1968.” LCNAF no2009019373.
sources.researchNote: The GND records Robert Péguy as a director born 14 December 1883 and deceased 21 July 1968, with the variants Péguy, Marcel Robert and Robert, Marcel; LCNAF agrees on the years 1883–1968. The French Wikipedia article gives the birth name as Marcel Robert Péguy and locates both his birth and death in the 17th arrondissement of Paris. Neither authority file records the spelling Pégy; the GND links directly to the filmportal.de record for the same man. The form printed in the credits of Son altesse l’amour is therefore treated as a source-specific spelling rather than as a name he is known to have used elsewhere.
sources.title: GND 1061685829 and LCNAF no2009019373 — Péguy, Robert
sources.creator: Deutsche Nationalbibliothek

sources.shortCitation: Authority records for Léo Lelièvre fils (1899–1966)
sources.fullCitation: Bibliothèque nationale de France. “Léo Lelièvre (1899–1966).” data.bnf.fr, ark:/12148/cb147911725. Library of Congress. “Lelièvre, Léo.” LCNAF n2010078826. Deutsche Nationalbibliothek. “Lelièvre, Léo.” GND 140364778X. Wikidata Q110225870.
sources.title: Léo Lelièvre (1899-1966)
sources.creator: Bibliothèque nationale de France
sources.researchNote: Two lyricists of the same name were at work in Paris in the 1930s: the chansonnier Léo Lelièvre (1872-1956), born in Reims, and his son Léo Edmond Lelièvre (1899-1966), a member of SACEM from November 1919, who wrote for the Casino de Paris beside Henri Varna and whose covers name him “Léo Lelièvre fils”, among them “Gosse de Paris” (1929) and “Le Tambour-major” from the revue “Paris qui brille” (1931). Both men worked on “Parade de France” in 1934: the Salabert prints of Maïotte Almaby’s créole numbers “La Vraie Créola” and “Ma Goulou Goulou” read “paroles françaises de Léo Lelièvre père”, while the Coda prints of the Jurmann–Kaper songs carry the undifferentiated form. The BnF catalogue is divided over those Coda prints: the notices for the illustrated issues and for the chant-et-piano prints of “C’est chez nous” and “Un baiser de femme sous un ciel de feu” link the son, whereas notices for three further printings of “Un baiser de femme sous un ciel de feu”, including Paul Saegel’s orchestral arrangement, still link the father. The son is preferred on three grounds: the printed “père” used for the other Lelièvre inside the same revue, the continuity of the Varna partnership at the Casino de Paris from 1929 onwards, and the weight of the revised catalogue notices.

sources.shortCitation: LCNAF and GND authority records for Helmuth Wolfes
sources.fullCitation: Library of Congress. “Wolfes, Helmuth, 1901–1971.” LCNAF n2009033210. Deutsche Nationalbibliothek. “Wolfes, Helmut.” Gemeinsame Normdatei, GND 117446882.
sources.title: Wolfes, Helmuth, 1901-1971
sources.creator: Library of Congress
sources.publication: Library of Congress Name Authority File (LCNAF)
sources.researchNote: The GND identifies him as a conductor and composer, born 22 April 1901 in Hanover and deceased 4 September 1971 in Cleveland, Ohio; it records Germany and the United States and identifies the United States as his place of exile. Its variant forms are Wolfes, Helmut Ernst and Wolfes, Helmuth. The heading is taken from the Library of Congress, which spells the forename Helmuth; the German form Helmut, under which he worked before emigration, remains the display name.
